identification.summary: Denim Tsunami is Microsoft's name for an Austria-based private-sector offensive actor (PSOA) that Microsoft previously tracked as KNOTWEED and identified as DSIRF [S1]. Microsoft says it observed the actor using multiple Windows and Adobe zero-day and n-day exploits to deploy a malware toolset called Subzero in limited, targeted attacks [S1]. Microsoft notes that open-source news reports had already attributed Subzero to DSIRF [S1][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft says KNOTWEED-linked infrastructure had been serving malware since at least February 2020 [S1][S2]. Exploit activity Microsoft describes dates to 2021 (CVE-2021-28550, CVE-2021-31199, CVE-2021-31201, CVE-2021-36948) [S1]. Netzpolitik published DSIRF's Subzero presentation in 2021 [S4].
identification.notes: Microsoft's update note on its original post states that KNOTWEED is now tracked as Denim Tsunami, part of its weather-themed taxonomy (update dated April 2023) [S1]. Microsoft's threat actor naming table lists DEV-0291 as an in-development designation for Denim Tsunami [S5]; the July 2022 post does not mention DEV-0291 [S1]. 'DSIRF' is the company name Microsoft links to the activity; Microsoft states the actor may blend access-as-a-service and hack-for-hire models [S1]. No MITRE ATT&CK group is recorded for this actor in the encyclopedia record.

attribution.sponsor: Not a state actor in Microsoft's reporting. Microsoft classifies the actor as a private-sector offensive actor and links it to the Austria-based company DSIRF [S1]. DSIRF stated that Subzero was developed exclusively for official use by EU states and is not offered or sold commercially [S3]. Which, if any, government customers used Subzero is not established in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft states 'multiple' links between KNOTWEED and DSIRF but does not publish a numeric or high/medium/low confidence label for the corporate attribution [S1]. Microsoft assesses with medium confidence that the Adobe Reader RCE in the 2022 chain was a zero-day [S1]. The DSIRF-to-KNOTWEED link is a Microsoft assessment, not a government attribution.
attribution.basis: Microsoft cites C2 infrastructure that directly links to DSIRF, a DSIRF-associated GitHub account used in one attack, a code-signing certificate issued to DSIRF used to sign an exploit, and open-source news reports attributing Subzero to DSIRF [S1]. Netzpolitik separately published DSIRF's own Subzero presentation in 2021 [S4].

objectives: Microsoft describes PSOAs as selling hacking tools or services through varied business models, and says this actor may blend access-as-a-service and hack-for-hire [S1]. Observed use was to gain access to and exfiltrate data from law firms, banks and strategic consultancies, with keylogging, screenshots, file theft and a remote shell [S1]. The end customer and purpose of individual intrusions are not stated in the sources [S1].

regions: Microsoft describes the affected customers as European and Central American [S1]
targeting.notes: Microsoft says a victim's country does not necessarily match the location of the actor's customer, and that it did not name victims [S1]. Microsoft confirmed with at least one Subzero victim that the activity was unauthorized (no red-team or penetration-test engagement) [S1].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft describes the Subzero toolset as follows. Corelump is the main in-memory payload with keylogging, screenshots, file exfiltration, a remote shell and plugins fetched from C2. Jumplump is a persistent loader using COM hijacking. Downloader shellcode hides its payload in a JPEG and decrypts it with RC4. PassLib steals credentials from browsers, email clients, LSASS, LSA secrets and the Windows credential manager. Mex bundles public tools including Mimikatz, Rubeus, SharpHound3 and Chisel [S1]. Exploits: CVE-2022-22047 (Windows CSRSS privilege escalation zero-day, patched July 2022) chained with an Adobe Reader RCE delivered in a PDF by email; in 2021 CVE-2021-28550 (Adobe Reader) with CVE-2021-31199 and CVE-2021-31201, and CVE-2021-36948 (Windows Update Medic Service) loading a DLL signed by 'DSIRF GmbH'; and a real-estate-themed Excel file with obfuscated VBA and Excel 4.0 macros [S1][S2]. Infrastructure was largely hosted at Digital Ocean and Choopa, and tools were fetched from public file shares [S1].

campaigns.name: Subzero marketing and pre-exposure period
campaigns.summary: Netzpolitik reported in 2021 on a DSIRF presentation describing Subzero as a tool to hack and monitor computers and smartphones, and on a 2018 email forwarding DSIRF's profile to Jan Marsalek, then a Wirecard board member. DSIRF's managing director told Netzpolitik that Subzero had not yet been used operationally or sold commercially [S4].

campaigns.name: Earliest infrastructure activity
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says KNOTWEED-linked infrastructure (largely Digital Ocean and Choopa hosting) has been active since at least February 2020 [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Windows and Adobe exploit chains
campaigns.summary: Microsoft links the actor to CVE-2021-28550 (Adobe Reader) with CVE-2021-31199 and CVE-2021-31201 (Windows privilege escalation), all patched June 2021, and to CVE-2021-36948 (Windows Update Medic Service), which loaded a DLL signed by DSIRF GmbH [S1].

campaigns.name: Microsoft public disclosure of KNOTWEED and CVE-2022-22047
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published its analysis tying KNOTWEED to DSIRF, reporting attacks on law firms, banks and strategic consultancies in Austria, the UK and Panama using a Windows zero-day (CVE-2022-22047, patched July 2022) and an Adobe Reader RCE. Microsoft added Defender detections and published IOCs and hunting queries [S1].

campaigns.name: DSIRF response and Austrian review
campaigns.summary: Press reported DSIRF stating that Subzero was developed exclusively for official use in EU states, is not offered or sold commercially, and that it had commissioned an independent expert and begun an internal review. Reporting also states Austria's interior ministry said its Directorate for State Protection and Intelligence was examining the allegations [S3].

campaigns.name: Renamed Denim Tsunami
campaigns.summary: Microsoft updated its post to state that KNOTWEED is now tracked as Denim Tsunami under its weather-themed naming taxonomy [S1].

diamond.adversary: Austria-based private-sector offensive actor linked by Microsoft to the company DSIRF; possible access-as-a-service and hack-for-hire model; end customers not identified [S1].
diamond.capability: Subzero toolset (Corelump, Jumplump, PassLib, Mex), Windows and Adobe zero-day and n-day exploit chains, COM hijacking persistence, and malicious Excel macros [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: C2 domains acrobatrelay[.]com, finconsult[.]cc and realmetaldns[.]com; hosting largely at Digital Ocean and Choopa; DSIRF-linked domains and a DSIRF-associated GitHub account; tooling pulled from public file shares such as vultrobjects[.]com [S1].
diamond.victim: Law firms, banks and strategic consultancies in Austria, the United Kingdom and Panama [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Commercial surveillance and intrusion-for-hire market; Microsoft frames such actors as 'cyber mercenaries' selling tools or services [S1]. DSIRF said Subzero was for EU government use only [S3]. Earlier press tied the firm to a former Wirecard executive [S4].
diamond.technology: Unpatched Windows and Adobe Reader software, email delivery of PDF and Excel lures, and Windows components exploitable for local privilege escalation (CSRSS, Windows Update Medic Service) [S1].

gaps: No identified end customers, operators or government clients; DSIRF's claim of EU-government-only use is unverified [S3].
Microsoft did not name victims or publish a confidence label for the DSIRF attribution [S1].

Whether the activity continued after July 2022 under another name or entity is not established in the sources gathered. A futurezone report states that DSIRF is closing; I could not open that article (host unreachable) and could not confirm its date or any successor company.
Outcome of the Austrian State Protection review and parliamentary inquiries is not confirmed; the ministry statement came via press coverage only [S3].
Netzpolitik, futurezone, BleepingComputer and Security Affairs pages could not be fetched directly; netzpolitik details rely on search-result summaries [S4].

DEV-0291 is listed in Microsoft's naming table but the July 2022 post does not use it; the precise relationship of the in-development designation to KNOTWEED is not documented in fetched sources [S1][S5].
Press reports of ownership structure (Liechtenstein parent, named individuals) were seen only in search summaries and are not included as facts here.
No MITRE ATT&CK group mapping was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain for this actor is Windows endpoints used by legal, financial and consulting staff, and email gateways that deliver PDF and Excel lures; these personnel hold privileged client and strategic-planning data [S1]. STEP 2: As a commercial supplier, the actor's capability is available to whichever customer pays, so the threat is a capability pool rather than a single sponsor; zero-day use narrows defender windows to the patch cycle [S1]. STEP 3: Observed template is a PDF or Excel lure, then an Adobe Reader or macro foothold, then a Windows privilege-escalation exploit, then an in-memory implant (Corelump) with COM-hijack persistence and credential theft (PassLib, Mex) [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume, targeted intrusions against professional-services firms in Europe and Latin America on behalf of unidentified customers. MDCOA is use of the same toolset or a successor against contractors or advisers supporting government or defense planning, where a customer's interest aligns with adversary state priorities (not shown in the sources). Candidate indicators: Defender detections named in Microsoft's post (Jumplump, Corelump, Mexlib, Medcerc), unexpected COM hijacks, JPEG downloads with encrypted payloads, and the published C2 domains [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track disclosures of zero-days from PSOAs in Windows and Adobe products and feed patch status into the common operational picture [S1]. (2) Authorities: activity against private-sector victims in allied countries is typically a law-enforcement or partner-nation matter; coordinate through established CTI-sharing channels rather than assuming a DoD response authority. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize patching of CSRSS and Adobe Reader-class vulnerabilities on mission-support endpoints, restrict Excel 4.0 macros, and hunt for COM hijacking [S1]. (4) Coordination: share Microsoft-published IOCs and queries with DIB and contractor partners and with the cyber protection teams supporting law, finance and consulting providers [S1].
